entries.298f61b11ade5ae8dc11a4934bac885687ff46a0: <div eID="gen19679" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen19680" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen19681" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen19681" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen19680" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen19682" type="x-p"/> The psalmist, in great straits, prays for his personal safety, <reference osisRef="Psa.35.1-Psa.35.3">Psa 35:1-3</reference>; and for the confusion of his enemies, <reference osisRef="Psa.35.4-Psa.35.8">Psa 35:4-8</reference>; expresses has confidence in God, <reference osisRef="Psa.35.9">Psa 35:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.35.10">Psa 35:10</reference>; mentions his kindness to those who had rewarded him evil for his good, <reference osisRef="Psa.35.11-Psa.35.16">Psa 35:11-16</reference>; appeals to God against them, <reference osisRef="Psa.35.17-Psa.35.26">Psa 35:17-26</reference>; prays for those who befriended him; and praises God for his goodness, <reference osisRef="Psa.35.27">Psa 35:27</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.35.28">Psa 35:28</reference>. <div eID="gen19682" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19683" type="x-p"/> There is nothing in the title worthy of remark. The Psalm is simply attributed to David, and was most probably of his composing; and refers to the time of his persecution by Saui and his courtiers. The Syriac says it was composed when the Idumeans attacked David. The Arabic says it is a prophecy concerning the incarnation, and concerning the things practiced against Jeremiah by the people. Some think that our Lord's sufferings are particularly pointed out here; and Bishop Horsley thinks that <reference osisRef="Psa.35.11-Psa.35.16">Psa 35:11-16</reference> apply more literally and exactly to Christ than to any other whomsoever. <div eID="gen19683" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19684" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen19684" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19685" type="x-p"/> Plead my cause, O Lord - Literally, Contend, Lord, with then that contend with me. The word is often used in a forensic or law sense.
entries.44b668ee6badecdf51adecfd35278ae96f647f06: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen19685" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19686" type="x-p"/> Take hold of shield and buckler - Let them be discomfited in battle who are striving to destroy my life. It is by the shield and buckler of others, not any of his own that God overthrows the enemies of his people. This is spoken merely after the manner of men.
entries.04e0ca2fa32240073139b3e4d1d17bf723db1ace: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen19686" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19687" type="x-p"/> Say unto my soul, I am thy salvation - Give me an assurance that thou wilt defend both body and soul against my adversaries.
entries.3271abb4a46b567923760cc175c7768dc4335023: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen19687" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19688" type="x-p"/> Let then be confounded - Let none of their projects or devices against me succeed. Blast all their designs. <div eID="gen19688" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19689" type="x-p"/> The imprecations in these verses against enemies are all legitimate. They are not against the souls or eternal welfare of those sinners, but against their schemes and plans for destroying the life of an innocent man; and the holiest Christian may offer up such prayers against his adversaries. If a man aim a blow at another with a design to take away his life, and the blow would infallibly be mortal if it took place, and the person about to be slain see that by breaking the arm of his adversary he may prevent his own death, and thus save his enemy from actual murder; it is his duty to prevent this double evil by breaking the arm of the blood-thirsty man. It is on this principle that David prays against his adversaries in the first eight verses of this Psalm.
entries.791c263bf7b4640c0a605f23ce92c9b725c7fb2c: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen19689" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19690" type="x-p"/> Let the angel of the Lord chase them - By angel we may either understand one of those spirits, whether good or bad, commonly thus denominated, or any thing used by God himself as the instrument of their confusion.
entries.13fe923f65bbeb0135763f87f832511404f10eb7: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen19690" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19691" type="x-p"/> Let their way be dark - Let them lose their way, be entangled in morasses and thickets, and be confounded in all their attempts to injure me. All these phrases are military; and relate to ambushes, hidden snares, forced marches in order to surprise, and stratagems of different kinds.
entries.19f9efa40edea61dc16f2f7e8c7ac5f69e489b1a: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen19691" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19692" type="x-p"/> For without cause have they hid for me their net in a pit - The word שחת shachath, a pit, belongs to the second member of this verse, and the whole should be read thus: For without a cause they have hidden for me their net, without a cause they have digged a pit for my life. They have used every degree and species of cunning and deceit to ruin me.
entries.5b729ead5bcb1d4b5e82b1e270f6ce542e45b824: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen19692" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19693" type="x-p"/> Let his net that he hath hid - See the notes on <reference osisRef="Psa.7.15">Psa 7:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.7.16">Psa 7:16</reference>.
entries.754bc3489611a7246aded84aef1ca597923fb838: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen19693" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19694" type="x-p"/> My soul - My life, thus saved: - <div eID="gen19694" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19695" type="x-p"/> Shall be joyful in the Lord - I am so circumstanced at present as to be in the utmost danger of being destroyed by my foes; if I escape, it must be by the strong arm of the Lord; and to him shall the glory be given.
entries.3f627e5ffff5926ef0cb7f0c55b22f300e44051e: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen19695" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19696" type="x-p"/> All my bones shall say - My life being preserved, all the members of my body shall magnify thy saving mercy. <div eID="gen19696" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19697" type="x-p"/> Deliverest the poor - This is a general maxim: God is peculiarly mindful of the poor. Where secular advantages are withheld, there is the more need for spiritual help. God considers this, and his kind providence works accordingly.
entries.513846f998f9bd46eeae3116f02c23ed2b41bfec: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen19697" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19698" type="x-p"/> False witnesses did rise up - There is no doubt that several of this kind were found to depose against the life of David; and we know that the wicked Jews employed such against the life of Christ. See <reference osisRef="Mat.26.59">Mat 26:59</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mat.26.60">Mat 26:60</reference>. <div eID="gen19698" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19699" type="x-p"/> They laid to my charge things that I knew not - They produced the most unfounded charges; things of which I had never before heard.
entries.9f7b7b99431db8ad35b6d6b603fc253aa54214bd: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen19699" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19700" type="x-p"/> To the spoiling of my soul - To destroy my life; so נפש nephesh should be translated in a multitude of places, where our translators have used the word soul.
entries.146704820e433bbfb3b5cf012a886b3fa9d0431f: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen19700" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19701" type="x-p"/> When they were sick - This might refer to the case of Absalom, who was much beloved of his father, and for whose life and prosperity he no doubt often prayed, wept, and fasted. <div eID="gen19701" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19702" type="x-p"/> My prayer returned into mine own bosom - Though from the wayward and profligate life they led, they did not profit by my prayers, yet God did not permit me to pray in vain. They were like alms given to the miserable for God's sake, who takes care to return to the merciful man tenfold into his bosom. The bosom is not only the place where the Asiatics carry their purses, but also where they carry any thing that is given to them.
entries.6febc548b31adee3a6b9be5c2ef5ff726478849c: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen19702" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19703" type="x-p"/> Mourneth for his mother - כאבל אם caabel em, as a mourning mother. How expressive is this word!
entries.788bfb51afae195b7a941b4031f5b59a50fa25d7: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen19703" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19704" type="x-p"/> But in mine adversity they reioiced - How David was mocked and insulted in the case of Absalom's rebellion by Shimei and others, is well known. <div eID="gen19704" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19705" type="x-p"/> The abjects - נכים nechim, the smiters, probably hired assassins. They were everywhere lying in wait, to take away my life.
entries.9222d95f66758b5776bf4665e240a4c94e1b1d39: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen19705" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19706" type="x-p"/> With hypocritical mockers in feasts - These verses seem to be prophetic of the treatment of Christ. They did tear me, and I knew it not. They blindfolded and buffeted him; they placed him in such circumstances as not to be able to discern who insulted him, except by a supernatural knowledge. With hypocritical mockers in feasts may also relate prophetically to our Lord's sufferings. Herod clothed him in a purple robe, put a reed in his hand for a scepter, bowed the knee before him, and set him at naught. Here their hypocritical conduct (pretending one thing while they meant another) was manifest, and possibly; this occurred at one of Herod's feasts.
entries.847b911dd87e09b7fda2fe2c1fd573a71800ceb9: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen19706" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19707" type="x-p"/> My darling - יחידתי yechidathi, my only one, <reference osisRef="Psa.22.20">Psa 22:20</reference>. My united one, or He that is alone. Perhaps this may relate to Christ. See the note on <reference osisRef="Psa.22.20">Psa 22:20</reference>.
entries.062e0c798bda10fc9a9af16a89241e3bcbc38445: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen19707" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19708" type="x-p"/> I will give thee thanks in the great congregation - I hope to be able to attend at the tabernacle with thy followers, and there publicly express my gratitude for the deliverance thou hast given me.
entries.3f756b901c07ae4ca63a2fcbc60fe6e2fae668bf: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen19708" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19709" type="x-p"/> That are mine enemies - Saul and his courtiers.
entries.8d5f8b115218d2fd4be218dfd0bc621b2fa6a20c: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen19709" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19710" type="x-p"/> They opened their mouth wide - Gaped upon me to express their contempt. <div eID="gen19710" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19711" type="x-p"/> And said, Aha, aha, our eye hath seen it - They said, האח האח heach, heach, the last syllable in each word being a protracted strongly guttural sound, marking insult and triumph at the same time. It is the word which we translate Ah, <reference osisRef="Psa.35.25">Psa 35:25</reference>.
entries.600769a1f888bd7eaa9d9f4581967ca999ebfe72: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen19711" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19712" type="x-p"/> This thou hast seen - I have no need to adduce evidences of these wrongs; thou, to whom I appeal, hast seen them. Therefore,
entries.bb49743462100c37360a11fce333568036892705: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen19712" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19713" type="x-p"/> Stir up thyself, and awake to my judgment - I have delivered my cause into thy hand, and appeal to thee as my Judge; and by thy decision I am most willing to abide.
entries.f062e3d7eb262523c9dc5ea81e64c4e9bdb3451d: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen19713" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19714" type="x-p"/> Judge me, O Lord my God - The manner of his appeal shows the strong confidence he had in his own innocence.
entries.5cfe12a5c2ed6cc662eaf083d7e451650c284bcf: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen19714" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19715" type="x-p"/> Swallowed him up - בלענוהו billaanuhu, we have gulped him down.
entries.c31d07e361847fca33c9707f7b634bb5af4e05e2: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen19715" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19716" type="x-p"/> Let them be ashamed - This may be a prophetic declaration against Saul and his courtiers. They were ashamed, confounded, clothed with shame, and dishonored. All these took place in Saul's last battle with the Philistines, where he lost his crown and his life, and came to a most dishonorable end.
entries.faada33ba696cd24d2da50f76a7c8df655eae0e7: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen19716" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19717" type="x-p"/> Let them shout for joy and be glad - While my enemies are confounded, let my friends exult in the Lord; and let them all praise him for his marvellous kindness to me.
entries.10217f231fbcd5d313febf5ac7533001b208d48d: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen19717" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19718" type="x-p"/> And my tongue shall speak - I, who am chiefly concerned, and who have received most, am under the greatest obligation; and it will require the constant gratitude and obedience of my whole life to discharge the mighty debt I owe.  <chapter eID="Ps.35"/> <div eID="gen19718" type="x-p"/>

entries.374ff2edde8699df7c0f61a62577fe51c5fb3dc4: <div eID="gen9385" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Call to Arms against Ungrateful Persecutors, Addressed to God</title> <div sID="gen9386" type="x-p"/> This Psalms 35 and Ps 34 form a pair. They are the only Psalms in which the name מלאך יהוה is mentioned. The Psalms that belong to the time of David’s persecution by Saul are the Psalms which are more especially pervaded by such retrospective references to the Tôra. And in fact this whole Psalm is, as it were, the lyrical expansion of that which David expresses before Saul in 1Sa 24:15. The critical opinion as to the authorship of this Psalm is closely allied with that respecting the author of Ps 40 and 69 to which Ps 35 is nearly related; cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.35.21">Psa 35:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.35.27">Psa 35:27</reference> with Psa 40:16.; <reference osisRef="Ps.35.13">Psa 35:13</reference> with Psa 69:11.; whereas the relation of Ps 71 to Ps 35 is decidedly a secondary one. Hitzig conjectures it to be Jeremiah; but <reference osisRef="Ps.35.1">Psa 35:1</reference> are appropriate in the lips of a persecuted king, and not of a persecuted prophet. The points of contact of the writings of Jeremiah with our Psalm (Jer 18:19., <reference osisRef="Jer.23.12">Jer 23:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lam.2.16">Lam 2:16</reference>), may therefore in this instance be more safely regarded as reminiscences of an earlier writer than in Ps 69. Throughout the whole Psalm there prevails a deep vexation of spirit (to which corresponds the suffix  מו-, as in Ps 59; <reference osisRef="Ps.56.1-Ps.56.13">Psa 56:1-13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.11.1-Ps.11.7">Psa 11:1-7</reference>; Psa 17:1-15; 22; <reference osisRef="Ps.64.1-Ps.64.10">Psa 64:1-10</reference>) and strong emotion; it is not until the second part, where the poet describes the base ingratitude of his enemies, that the language becomes more clam and transparent, and a more quiet sadness takes the place of indignation and rage. <div eID="gen9386" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9387" type="x-p"/> Each of the three parts opens with a cry for deliverance; and closes, in the certain assumption that it will take place, with a vow of thanksgiving. The divisions cannot therefore be mistaken, viz., <reference osisRef="Ps.35.1">Psa 35:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.35.11">Psa 35:11</reference>, Psa 35:19. The relative numbers of the stichs in the separate groups is as follows: 6. 6. 5. 5. 7. 7. 5. 6. 6. 6. 5. <div eID="gen9387" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9388" type="x-p"/> There are only a few Psalms of David belonging to the time of Saul’s persecution, which, like Ps 22, keep within the limits of deep inward grief; and in scarcely a single instance do we find him confining himself to the expression of the accursed fate of his enemies with prophetic certainty, as that which he confidently expects will be realised (as, e.g., in <reference osisRef="Ps.7.13-Ps.7.17">Psa 7:13-17</reference>). But for the most part the objective announcement of punishment is swallowed up by the force of his inmost feelings, and changed into the most importunate prayer (as in <reference osisRef="Ps.7.7">Psa 7:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.17.13">Psa 17:13</reference>, and frequently); and this feverish glow of feeling becomes still more harshly prominent, when the prayer for the revelation of divine judgment in punishment passes over into a wish that it may actually take place. In this respect Ps 7, 35, 69, 109 form a fearful gradation. In Ps 109, the old expositors count as many as thirty anathemas. What explanation can we give of such language coming from the lips and heart of the poet? Perhaps as paroxysms of a desire for revenge? His advance against Nabal shows that even a David was susceptible of such feelings; but 1Sa 25:32. also shows that only a gentle stirring up of his conscience was needed to dissuade him from it. How much more natural-we throw out this consideration in agreement with Kurtz - that the preponderance of that magnanimity peculiar to him should have maintained its ascendancy in the moments of the highest religious consecration in which he composed his Psalms! It is inconceivable that the unholy fire of personal passion could be here mingled with the holy fire of his love to God. It is in fact the Psalms more especially, which are the purest and most faithful mirror of the piety of the Old Testament: the duty of love towards one’s enemies, however, is so little alien to the Old Testament (Exo 23:4., <reference osisRef="Lev.19.18">Lev 19:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.20.22">Pro 20:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.24.17">Pro 24:17</reference>; Pro 25:21., Job 31:29.), that the very words of the Old Testament are made use of even in the New to inculcate this love. And from Ps 7, in its agreement with the history of his conduct towards Saul, we have seen that David was conscious of having fulfilled this duty. All the imprecatory words in these Psalms come, therefore, from the pure spring of unself-seeking zeal for the honour of God. That this zeal appears in this instance as zeal for his own person or character arises from the fact, that David, as the God-anointed heir of the kingdom, stands in antagonism to Saul, the king alienated from God; and, that to his mind the cause of God, the continuance of the church, and the future of Israel, coincide with his own destiny. The fire of his anger is kindled at this focus (so to speak) of the view which he has of his own position in the course of the history of redemption. It is therefore a holy fire; but the spirit of the New Testament, as Jesus Himself declare sin <reference osisRef="Luke.9.55">Luk 9:55</reference>, is in this respect, nevertheless, a relatively different spirit from that of the Old. That act of divine love, redemption, out of the open fountain of which there flowed forth the impulse of a love which embraces and conquers the world, was then as yet not completed; and a curtain then still hung before eternity, before heaven and hell, so that imprecations like <reference osisRef="Ps.69.20">Psa 69:20</reference> were not understood,even by him who uttered them, in their infinite depth of meaning. Now that this curtain is drawn up, the New Testament faith shrinks back from invoking upon any one a destruction that lasts לעולם; and love seeks, so long as a mere shadow of possibility exists, to rescue everything human from the perdition of an unhappy future-a perdition the full meaning of which cannot be exhausted by human thought. <div eID="gen9388" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9389" type="x-p"/> In connection with all this, however, there still remains one important consideration. The curses, which are contained in the Davidic Psalms of the time of Saul’s persecution, are referred to in the New Testament as fulfilled in the enemies of Jesus Christ, <reference osisRef="Acts.1.20">Act 1:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.11.7">Rom 11:7</reference>-10. One expression found in our Psalm, ἐμίσησάν με δωρεάν (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.69.5">Psa 69:5</reference>) is used by Jesus (Joh 15:25) as fulfilled in Him; it therefore appears as though the whole Psalm ought to be, or at least may be, taken typically as the words of Christ. But nowhere in the Gospels do we read an imprecation used by Jesus against His own and the enemies of the kingdom of God; David’s imprecations are not suited to the lips of the Saviour, nor do the instances in which they are cited in the New Testament give them the impress of being His direct words: they are treated as the language of prophecy by virtue of the Spirit, whose instrument David was, and whose work the Scriptures are. And it is only in this sense that the Christian adopts them in prayer. For after the pattern of his Lord, who on the cross prayed “Father forgive them,” he desires that even his bitterest enemies may not be eternally lost, but, though it be only when <hi type="italic">in articulo mortis</hi>, that they may come to their right mind. Even the anathemas of the apostle against the Judaising false teachers and against Alexander the smith (<reference osisRef="Gal.1.9">Gal 1:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.5.12">Gal 5:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.14">2Ti 4:14</reference>), refer only to temporal removal and chastisement, not to eternal perdition. They mark the extreme boundary where, in extraordinary instances, the holy zeal of the New Testament comes in contact with the holy fervour of the Old Testament.
entries.1517da7b898429efd4a4a3915c7017c179d1ea00: <reference osisRef="Ps.35.1-Ps.35.3">Psa 35:1-3</reference> <div eID="gen9389" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9390" type="x-p"/> The psalmist begins in a martial and anthropomorphical style such as we have not hitherto met with. On the ultima-accentuation of ריבה, vid., on Psa 3:8. Both את are signs of the accusative. This is a more natural rendering here, where the psalmist implores God to subjugate his foes, than to regard את as equivalent to עם (cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.49.25">Isa 49:25</reference> with <hi type="italic">ib</hi>. <reference osisRef="Ps.27.8">Psa 27:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.10.2">Job 10:2</reference>); and, moreover, for the very same reason the expression in this instance is לחם, (in the <hi type="italic">Kal</hi>, which otherwise only lends the <hi type="italic">part</hi>. לחם, Psa 56:2., to the <hi type="italic">Niph</hi>. נלחם) instead of the reciprocal form הלּחם. It is usually supposed that לחם means properly <hi type="italic">vorare</hi>, and war is consequently conceived of as a devouring of men; but the Arabic offers another primary meaning: to press close and compact (<hi type="italic">Niph</hi>. to one another), consequently מלחמה means a dense crowd, a dense bustle and tumult (cf. the Homeric κλόνος). The summons to Jahve to arm, and that in a twofold manner, viz., with the מגן for warding off the hostile blow and צנּה (vid., Ps 5:13) which covers the body like a <hi type="italic">testudo</hi> - by which, inasmuch as it is impossible to hold both shields at the same time, the figure is idealised - is meant to express, that He is to make Himself felt by the foes, in every possible way, to their own confounding, as the unapproachable One. The ב of בּעזרתי (in the character of help turned towards me) is the so-called <hi type="italic">Beth essentiae</hi>,<note placement="foot">The Hebrew <hi type="italic">Beth essentiae</hi> is used much more freely and extensively than the Arabic, which is joined exclusively to the predicate of a simple clause, where in our language the verb is “to be,” and as a rule only to the predicate of negative clauses: <hi type="italic">laisa bi - hakı̂mim</hi>, he is not wise, or <hi type="italic">laisa bi - l - hakı̂mi</hi>, he is not the wise man. The predicate can accordingly be indeterminate or determinate. Moreover, in Hebrew, where this ב is found with the predicate, with the complement of the subject, or even, though only as a solecism (vid., Gesenius’ Thesaurus p. 175), with the subject itself, the word to which it is prefixed may be determinate, whether as an attribute determined by itself (<reference osisRef="Exod.6.3">Exo 6:3</reference>, בּאל שׁדּי), by a suffix (as above, <reference osisRef="Ps.35.2">Psa 35:2</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.146.5">Psa 146:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.18.4">Exo 18:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.3.26">Pro 3:26</reference>), or even by the article. At all events no syntactic objection can be brought against the interpretations of בעשׁן, “in the quality of smoke,” <reference osisRef="Ps.37.20">Psa 37:20</reference>; cf. בּהבל, <reference osisRef="Ps.78.33">Psa 78:33</reference>, and of בּנּפשׁ, “in the character of the soul,” Lev 17:11.</note> as in <reference osisRef="Exod.18.4">Exo 18:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.3.26">Pro 3:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.48.10">Isa 48:10</reference> (<hi type="italic">tanquam argentum</hi>), and frequently. הריק has the same meaning as in <reference osisRef="Exod.15.9">Exo 15:9</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Gen.14.14">Gen 14:14</reference>, viz., to bring forth, draw forth, to draw or unsheath (a sword); for as a sword is sheathed when not in use, so a spear is kept in the δουροδόκη (<hi type="italic">Odyss</hi>. i. 128). Even Parchon understands סגר to mean a weapon; and the word σάγαρις, in Herodotus, Xenophon, and Strabo, a northern Asiatic, more especially a Scythian, battle-axe, has been compared here;<note placement="foot">Probably one and the same word with the Armenian <hi type="italic">sakr</hi>, to which are assigned the (Italian) meanings <hi type="italic">mannaja, scure, brando ferro</hi>, in Ciakciak’s Armenian Lexicon; cf. Lagarde’s <hi type="italic">Gesammelte Abhandlungen</hi>, 1866, S. 203.</note> but the battle-axe was not a Hebrew weapon, and סגר, which, thus defectively written, has the look of an imperative, also gives the best sense when so taken (lxx σύγκλεισον, Targ. וּטרוק), viz., close, i.e., cut off, <hi type="italic">interclude</hi> scil. <hi type="italic">viam</hi>. The word has <hi type="italic">Dechî</hi>, because לקראת רדפי, “casting Thyself against my persecutors,” belongs to both the preceding summonses. Dachselt rightly directs attention to the similar sequence of the accents in <reference osisRef="Ps.55.19">Psa 55:19</reference>; Psa 66:15. The Mosaic figure of Jahve as a man of war (אישׁ מלחמה, <reference osisRef="Exod.15.3">Exo 15:3</reference>; Deu 32:41.) is worked out here with brilliant colours, under the impulse of a wrathful spirit. But we see from <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.35.3">Psa 35:3</reference></hi> what a spiritual meaning, nevertheless, the whole description is intended to convey. In God’s intervention, thus manifested in facts, he would gladly hear His consolatory utterance to himself. The burden of his cry is that God’s love may break through the present outward appearance of wrath and make itself felt by him.
entries.a1245d35d413b7d65f061817298f139dbfcaf29f: <reference osisRef="Ps.35.4-Ps.35.8">Psa 35:4-8</reference> <div eID="gen9390" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9391" type="x-p"/> Throughout the next two strophes follow terrible imprecations. According to Fürst and others the relation of בּושׁ and חפר is like that of <hi type="italic">erblassen</hi>, to turn pale (cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.29.22">Isa 29:22</reference> with <reference osisRef="Ps.34.6">Psa 34:6</reference>), and <hi type="italic">erröthen</hi>, to turn red, to blush. בושׁ has, however, no connection with בוץ, nor has חפר, Arab. <hi type="italic">chfr, chmr</hi>, any connection with Arab. <hi type="italic">hmr</hi>, to be red; but, according to its radical notion, בּושׁ means <hi type="italic">disturbari</hi> (vid., Ps 6:11), and חפר, <hi type="italic">obtegere, abscondere</hi> (vid., <reference osisRef="Ps.34.6">Psa 34:6</reference>). יסּגוּ, properly “let them be made to fall back” (cf. e.g., <reference osisRef="Isa.42.17">Isa 42:17</reference>). On the figure on <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.35.5">Psa 35:5</reference></hi> cf. Psa 83:14. The clauses respecting the Angel of Jahve, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.35.5">Psa 35:5</reference></hi> and <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.35.6">Psa 35:6</reference></hi>, are circumstantial clauses, viz., clauses defining the manner. דּחה (giving, viz., them, the push that shall cause their downfall, equivalent to דּחם or דּחם, <reference osisRef="Ps.68.28">Psa 68:28</reference>) is closely connected with the figure in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.35.6">Psa 35:6</reference></hi>, and רדפם, with the figure in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.35.5">Psa 35:5</reference></hi>; consequently it seems as though the original position of these two clauses respecting the Angel of Jahve had been disturbed; just as in Ps 34, the ע strophe and the פ strophe have changed their original places. It is the Angel, who took off Pharaoh’s chariot wheels so that they drave them heavily (<reference osisRef="Exod.14.25">Exo 14:25</reference>) that is intended here. The fact that this Angel is concerned here, where the point at issue is whether the kingship of the promise shall be destroyed at its very beginning or not, harmonises with the appearing of the מלאך ה at all critical junctures in the course of the history of redemption. חלקלקּות, <hi type="italic">loca passim lubrica</hi>, is an intensive form of expression for חלקות rof noisserp, Psa 73:18. Just as דּחה recalls to mind Ex 15, so רדפם recalls Judg 5. In this latter passage the Angel of Jahve also appears in the midst of the conquerors who are pursuing the smitten foe, incarnate as it were in Deborah.
entries.f89893c46a79b0832bc26ac0238c487ff8156d77: <reference osisRef="Ps.35.9-Ps.35.10">Psa 35:9-10</reference> <div eID="gen9392" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9393" type="x-p"/> This strophe, with which the first part of the song closes, contains the logical apodosis of those imprecatory jussives. The downfall of the power that is opposed to God will be followed by the joy of triumph. The bones of the body, which elsewhere are mentioned as sharing only in the anguish of the soul (<reference osisRef="Ps.6.3">Psa 6:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.31.11">Psa 31:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.32.3">Psa 32:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.51.10">Psa 51:10</reference>), are here made to share (as also in <reference osisRef="Ps.51.10">Psa 51:10</reference>) in the joy, into which the anxiety, that agitated even the marrow of the bones, is changed. The joy which he experiences in his soul shall throb through every member of his body and multiply itself, as it were, into a choir of praiseful voices. כּל with a conjunctive accent and without <hi type="italic">Makkeph</hi>, as also in <reference osisRef="Prov.19.7">Pro 19:7</reference> (not כּל־, vid., the Masora in Baer’s <hi type="italic">Psalterium</hi> p. 133), is to be read <hi type="italic">cāl</hi> (with קמץ רחב, <hi type="italic">opp</hi>. קמץ חטוף) according to Kimchi. According to Lonzano, however, it is to be read <hi type="italic">col</hi>, the conjunctive accent having an equal power with <hi type="italic">Makkeph</hi>; but this view is false, since an accent can never be placed against <hi type="italic">Kametz</hi> <hi type="italic">chatuph</hi>. The exclamation מי כמוך is taken from <reference osisRef="Exod.15.11">Exo 15:11</reference>, where, according to the Masora, it is to be pointed מי כמוך, as Ben Naphtali also points it in the passage before us. The <hi type="italic">Dagesh</hi>, which is found in the former passage and is wanting here, sharpens and hardens at the same time; it requires that the expression should be emphatically pronounced (without there being any danger in this instance of its being slurred over); it does not serve to denote the closer connection, but to give it especial prominence. חזק ממּנוּ, stronger than he, is equivalent to: strong, whereas the other is weak, just as in <reference osisRef="Jer.31.11">Jer 31:11</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Hab.1.13">Hab 1:13</reference>, צדּיק ממּנוּ, righteous, whereas he is ungodly. The repetition of ועני is meant to say: He rescues the עני, who is אביון (poor) enough already, from him who would take even the few goods that he possesses.
entries.5850b26ca0648ffc91f67f812aff3c8a25e16143: <reference osisRef="Ps.35.11-Ps.35.16">Psa 35:11-16</reference> <div eID="gen9393" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9394" type="x-p"/> The second part begins with two strophes of sorrowful description of the wickedness of the enemy. The futures in <reference osisRef="Ps.35.11">Psa 35:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.35.12">Psa 35:12</reference> describe that which at present takes place. עדי חמס are μάρτυρες ἄδικοι (lxx). They demand from him a confession of acts and things which lie entirely outside his consciousness and his way of acting (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.69.5">Psa 69:5</reference>): they would gladly brand him as a perjurer, as an usurper, and as a plunderer. What David complains of in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.35.12">Psa 35:12</reference></hi>, we hear Saul confess in <reference osisRef="1Sam.24.18">1Sa 24:18</reference>; the charge of ingratitude is therefore well-grounded. שׁכול לנפשׁי is not dependent on ישׁלּמוּני, in which case one would have looked for כּשׁול rather than שׁכול, but a substantival clause: “bereavement is to my soul,” its condition is that of being forsaken by all those who formerly showed me marks of affection; all these have, as it were, died off so far as I am concerned. Not only had David been obliged to save his parents by causing them to flee to Moab, but Michal was also torn from him, Jonathan removed, and all those at the court of Saul, who had hitherto sought the favour and friendship of the highly-gifted and highly-honoured son-in-law of the king, were alienated from him. And how sincerely and sympathisingly had he reciprocated their leanings towards himself! By ואני in <reference osisRef="Ps.35.13">Psa 35:13</reference>, he contrasts himself with the ungrateful and unfeeling ones. Instead of לבשׁתּי שׁק, the expression is לבוּשׁי שׁק; the tendency of poetry for the use of the substantival clause is closely allied to its fondness for well-conceived brevity and pictorial definition. He manifested towards them a love which knew no distinction between the <hi type="italic">ego</hi> and <hi type="italic">tu</hi>, which regarded their sorrow and their guilt as his own, and joined with them in their expiation for it; his head was lowered upon his breast, or he cowered, like Elijah (1Ki 18:42), upon the ground with his head hanging down upon his breast even to his knees, so that that which came forth from the inmost depths of his nature returned again as it were in broken accents into his bosom. Riehm’s rendering, “at their ungodliness and hostility my prayer for things not executed came back,” is contrary to the connection, and makes one look for אלי instead of אל־חיקי. Perret-Gentil correctly renders it, <hi type="italic">Je priai la tête penchée sur la poitrine</hi>. <div eID="gen9394" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9395" type="x-p"/> The Psalmist goes on to say in <reference osisRef="Ps.35.14">Psa 35:14</reference>, I went about as for a friend, for a brother to me, i.e., as if the sufferer had been such to me. With התחלּך, used of the solemn slowness of gait, which corresponds to the sacredness of pain, alternates שׁחח used of the being bowed down very low, in which the heavy weight of pain finds expression. כּאבל־אם, not: like the mourning (from אבל, like הבל from הבל) of a mother (Hitzig), but, since a personal אבל is more natural, and next to the mourning for an only child the loss of a mother (cf. <reference osisRef="Gen.24.67">Gen 24:67</reference>) strikes the deepest wound: like one who mourns (אבל־,<note placement="foot">According to the old Babylonian reading (belonging to a period when <hi type="italic">Pathach</hi> and <hi type="italic">Segol</hi> were as yet not distinguished from one another), כּאבל (with the sign of <hi type="italic">Pathach</hi> and the stroke for <hi type="italic">Raphe</hi> below = <hi type="italic">ä</hi>); vid., Pinsker, <hi type="italic">Zur Geschichte des Karaismus</hi>, S. 141, and <hi type="italic">Einleitung</hi>, S. 118.</note> like לבן־, <reference osisRef="Gen.49.12">Gen 49:12</reference>, from אבל, construct state, like טמא) for a mother (the objective genitive, as in <reference osisRef="Gen.27.41">Gen 27:41</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.34.8">Deu 34:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.8.10">Amo 8:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.6.26">Jer 6:26</reference>). קדר signifies the colours, outward appearance, and attire of mourning: with dark clothes, with tearful unwashed face, and with neglected beard. But as for them - how do they act at the present time, when he finds himself in צלע (<reference osisRef="Ps.38.17">Psa 38:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.18.12">Job 18:12</reference>), a sideway direction, i.e., likely to fall (from צלע, Arab. <hi type="italic">ḍl‛</hi>, to incline towards the side)? They rejoice and gather themselves together, and this assemblage of ungrateful friends rejoicing over another’s misfortune, is augmented by the lowest rabble that attach themselves to them. The verb נכה means to smite; <hi type="italic">Niph</hi>. נכּא, <reference osisRef="Job.30.6">Job 30:6</reference>, to be driven forth with a whip, after which the lxx renders it μάστιγες, Symm. πλῆκται, and the Targum <hi type="italic">conterentes me verbis suis</hi>; cf. הכּה בּלשׂון, Jer 18:18. But נכים cannot by itself mean smiters with the tongue. The adjective נכה signifies elsewhere with רגלים, one who is smitten in the feet, i.e., one who limps or halts, and with רוּח, but also without any addition, in <reference osisRef="Isa.16.7">Isa 16:7</reference>, one smitten in spirit, i.e., one deeply troubled or sorrowful. Thus, therefore, נכים from נכה, like גּאים from גּאה, may mean smitten, men, i.e., men who are brought low or reduced (Hengstenberg). It might also, after the Arabic <hi type="italic">nawika</hi>, to be injured in mind, <hi type="italic">anwak</hi>, stupid, silly (from the same root נך, to prick, smite, wound, cf. <hi type="italic">ichtalla</hi>, to be pierced through = mad), be understood as those mentally deranged, enraged at nothing or without cause. But the former definition of the notion of the word is favoured by the continuation of the idea of the verbal adjective נכים by ולא ידעתּי, persons of whom I have hitherto taken no notice because they were far removed from me, i.e., men belonging to the dregs of the people (cf. <reference osisRef="Job.19.18">Job 19:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.30.1">Job 30:1</reference>). The addition of ולא ידעתי certainly makes Olshausen’s conjecture that we should read נכרים somewhat natural; but the expression then becomes tautological, and there are other instances also in which psalm-poesy goes beyond the ordinary range of words, in order to find language to describe that which is loathsome, in the most glaring way. פרע, to tear, rend in pieces, viz., with abusive and slanderous words (like Arab. <hi type="italic">qr‛</hi> II) also does not occur anywhere else. <div eID="gen9395" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9396" type="x-p"/> And what remarkable language we now meet with in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.35.16">Psa 35:16</reference></hi>! מעוג does not mean scorn or buffoonery, as Böttcher and Hitzig imagine,<note placement="foot">The Talmudic עגה (לשׁון), B. <hi type="italic">Sanhedrin</hi> 101 <hi type="italic">b</hi>, which is said to mean “a jesting way of speaking,” has all the less place here, as the reading wavers between עגה (עגא) and אגא.</note> but according to 1Ki 17:12, a cake of a round formation (like the Talmudic עגּה, a circle); לעג, jeering, jesting. Therefore לעגי מעוג means: mockers for a cake, i.e., those who for a delicate morsel, for the sake of dainty fare, make scornful jokes, viz., about me, the persecuted one, vile parasites; German <hi type="italic">Tellerlecker, Bratenriecher</hi>, Greek κνισσοκόλακες, ψωμοκόλακες, Mediaeval Latin <hi type="italic">buccellarii</hi>. This לעגי מלוג, which even Rashi interprets in substantially the same manner, stands either in a logical co-ordinate relation (vid., on <reference osisRef="Isa.19.11">Isa 19:11</reference>) or in a logical as well as grammatical subordinate relation to its <hi type="italic">regens</hi> חנפי. In the former case, it would be equivalent to: the profane, viz., the cake-jesters; in the latter, which is the more natural, and quite suitable: the profane (= the profanest, vid., <reference osisRef="Ps.45.13">Psa 45:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.29.19">Isa 29:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.7.24">Eze 7:24</reference>) among cake-jesters. The בּ is not the <hi type="italic">Beth</hi> of companionship or fellowship, to express which עם or את (Hos 7:5) would have been used, but <hi type="italic">Beth essentiae</hi> or the <hi type="italic">Beth</hi> of characterisation: in the character of the most abject examples of this class of men do they gnash upon him with their teeth. The gerund חרק (of the noise of the teeth being pressed together, like Arab. <hi type="italic">ḥrq</hi>, of the crackling of a fire and the grating of a file), which is used according to Ges. §131, 4, <hi type="italic">b</hi>, carries its subject in itself. They gnash upon him with their teeth after the manner of the profanest among those, by whom their neighbour’s honour is sold for a delicate morsel.
entries.9676026925885391ead86d660ba9de95e68de5d0: <reference osisRef="Ps.35.17-Ps.35.18">Psa 35:17-18</reference> <div eID="gen9396" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9397" type="x-p"/> Just as the first part of the Psalm closed with wishes, and thanksgiving for their fulfilment, so the second part also closes with a prayer and thanksgiving. כּמּה (compounded of כּ, <hi type="italic">instar</hi>, and the interrogative מה which is drawn into the genitive by it; Aramaic כּמא, Arabic <hi type="italic">kam</hi>, Hebrew, like בּמּה, with <hi type="italic">Dag. forte conjunct</hi>., properly: the total of what?), which elsewhere means <hi type="italic">quot</hi>, here has the signification of <hi type="italic">quousque</hi>, as in Job 7:19. משּׁאיהם from שׁאה, the plural of which may be both שׁאים and שׁאות (this latter, however, does not occur), like the plural of אימה, terror, אימים and אימות. The suffix, which refers to the enemies as the authors of the destructions (<reference osisRef="Prov.3.25">Pro 3:25</reference>), shows that it is not to be rendered “from their destroyers” (Hitzig). If God continues thus to look on instead of acting, then the destructions, which are passing over David’s soul, will utterly destroy it. Hence the prayer: lead it back, bring that back, which is already well night borne away to destruction. On יהידה vid., Psa 22:21. The כּפירים, which is intended literally in <reference osisRef="Ps.34.11">Psa 34:11</reference>, is here emblematical. אודך is the cohortative. עצוּם as a parallel word to רב always refers, according to the context, to strength of numbers or to strength of power.
entries.201b256610e076032d735d3cc21b3fc674c24b8b: <reference osisRef="Ps.35.19-Ps.35.21">Psa 35:19-21</reference> <div eID="gen9397" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9398" type="x-p"/> I the third part, <reference osisRef="Ps.35.19">Psa 35:19</reference> the description of the godlessness of his enemies is renewed; but the soul of the praying psalmist has become more tranquil, and accordingly the language also is more clear and moves on with its accustomed calmness. שׁקר and חנּם are genitives, having an attributive sense (vid., on <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.23">2Sa 22:23</reference>). The verb קרץ signifies both to pinch = nip, <reference osisRef="Job.33.6">Job 33:6</reference> (cf. the Arabic <hi type="italic">karada</hi>, to cut off), and to pinch together, compress = to wink, generally used of the eyes, but also of the lips, <reference osisRef="Prov.16.30">Pro 16:30</reference>, and always as an insidiously malicious gesture. אל rules over both members of the verse as in <reference osisRef="Ps.75.6">Psa 75:6</reference>, and frequently. שׁלום in <reference osisRef="Ps.35.20">Psa 35:20</reference> is the word for whatever proceeds from good intentions and aims at the promotion or restoration of a harmonious relationship. רגעי־ארץ (from רגע, cf. ענוי־ארץ, <reference osisRef="Ps.76.10">Psa 76:10</reference>, Zep 2:3, צפוּניך, <reference osisRef="Ps.83.4">Psa 83:4</reference>) are those who quietly and unostentatiously walk in the ways of God. Against such they devise mischievous, lying slanders and accusations. And with wide-opened mouth, i.e., haughty scorn, they cry, as they carouse in sight of the misfortune of those they have persecuted: now we have that which we have longed to see. האח (composed of ההּ and אח) is a cry of joy, and more especially of malignant joy at another’s hurt (cf. <reference osisRef="Ezek.25.3">Eze 25:3</reference>).
entries.652d7f4b57f76b1eb430f9c02bd6cf761e99cab5: <reference osisRef="Ps.35.22-Ps.35.24">Psa 35:22-24</reference> <div eID="gen9398" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9399" type="x-p"/> The poet takes up this malignant “now our eye sees it” and gives another turn to it. With יהוה, alternates in <reference osisRef="Ps.35.22">Psa 35:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.35.23">Psa 35:23</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.35.17">Psa 35:17</reference>, אדני, the pronominal force of which is revived in the combination אלחי ואדני (vid., <reference osisRef="Ps.16.2">Psa 16:2</reference>). חעיר, carrying its object within itself, signifies to stir, rouse up, and הקיץ, to break off, tear one’s self away, gather one’s self up from, sleep. “To my right,” viz., to prove it by facts; “to my cause,” to carry it on in my defence.
entries.e0e425ccd677a1adfa307369cf7c7ca43224aefd: <reference osisRef="Ps.35.25-Ps.35.26">Psa 35:25-26</reference> <div eID="gen9399" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9400" type="x-p"/> On the metonymical use of נפשׁ, like τὸ ὀρεκτικόν for ὄρεξις, vid., <hi type="italic">Psychol</hi>. S. 203 tr. p. 239. The climax of desire is to swallow David up, i.e., to overpower him and clear him out of the way so that there is not a trace of him left. בּלּענוּהוּ with ע before נ, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.132.6">Psa 132:6</reference>, and frequently; on the law of the vowels which applies to this, vid., Ewald, §60, <hi type="italic">a</hi>. שׂמחי רעתי is a short form of expression for רעתי שׂמחים (בּ) על. To put on shame and dishonour (<reference osisRef="Ps.109.29">Psa 109:29</reference>, cf. Ps 18), so that these entirely cover them, and their public external appearance corresponds with their innermost nature.
entries.074550a57303c3fc70417f04419dc32554a4a210: <reference osisRef="Ps.35.27-Ps.35.28">Psa 35:27-28</reference> <div eID="gen9400" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9401" type="x-p"/> Those who wish that David’s righteousness may be made manifest and be avenged are said to take delight in it. When this takes place, Jahve’s righteousness is proved. יגדּל, let Him be acknowledged and praised as great, i.e., let Him be magnified! David desires that all who remain true to him may thus speak; and he, on his part, is determined to stir up the revelation of God’s righteousness in his heart, and to speak of that of which his heart is full (<reference osisRef="Ps.71.24">Psa 71:24</reference>).  <chapter eID="Ps.35"/> <div eID="gen9401" type="x-p"/>

PSALM 35.
So long as Saul was the enemy of David, the nobles, and such as at that time bore any authority, had (according to the subservient spirit which always prevails in the courts of kings) eagerly conspired to destroy an innocent man. They had also succeeded in inducing the common people to participate with them in their hatred and cruelty, so that all of them, from the highest to the lowest, burned with implacable hatred against him. But as he knew that the greatest part of them were thoughtlessly impelled to this by error and folly, and ignorance of the true state of affairs, he accounts those only his enemies who, from deliberate malice and wickedness, endeavored in this way to please Saul, in order to obtain his favor. Against them he calls upon God for vengeance. And, first, as he was conscious of no crime, he alleges his innocence before God; and, secondly, as they sought to inflict unmerited punishment upon him, he implores God for deliverance. After he has complained of their impious cruelty, he calls down upon them the punishment which they deserved. Moreover, as in confident reliance upon the oracle of God, which had been spoken by Samuel, and the holy anointing, he hoped for a better issue, he intersperses throughout the psalm testimonies of his thankfulness. Finally, he concludes the psalm by saying, that after he has been delivered, he will celebrate the praises of God all his life.
A Psalm of David.
Psalm 35:1-3
1. Plead my cause, O Jehovah! with them that plead against me; fight against them who fight against me. 2. Take the shield and the buckler, and rise up for my help. 3. Bring forth the spear, and oppose my persecutors: say unto my soul, “I am thy salvation.”
 
1. Plead my cause, O Jehovah! As the enemies of David not only avowedly sought to take away his life, but also troubled him by calumny and misrepresentation, he pleads for the redress of both these grievances. In the first place, by appealing to God for his aid in defense of his cause, he intimates, that he has to do with wicked and maligning men. In the second place, by urging him to take up arms, he shows that he was grievously oppressed. It was a very dishonorable thing, that this holy man, alike eminent for his beneficence and inoffensiveness towards all men, and who by his courtesy and meekness had merited, both in public and private, the esteem and favor of all, was not permitted to escape the reproach and calumny of wicked men; but it is important for us to know this, and it sets before us a very profitable example. If even David did not escape the malice of wicked men, it ought not to seem wonderful or strange to us, if they blame and bite at us. The injuries they inflict upon us may be grievous and painful, but there is incomparable consolation presented to us in this consideration, that God himself interposes for our protection and defense against false accusations. Though calumniators, then, should arise, and tear us, as it were, to pieces, by falsely charging us with crimes, we need not be disturbed, so long as God undertakes to plead our cause against them. There can be no doubt, that in the second clause of the verse David implores God to resist the armed violence of his enemies. The amount of the whole is, that being falsely accused and cruelly persecuted, and finding no help at the hands of men, the Prophet commits the preservation of his life and his reputation to God.
